title: Do autistic brains show the connectivity signature of aphantasia? Fusiform imagery node to frontoparietal connectivity in ABIDE I
description: [DRAFT FOR IVAN TO REWRITE] Visual mental imagery depends on a small region of the left fusiform gyrus, the fusiform imagery node (FIN), working together with left frontoparietal regions. In people with lifelong aphantasia (no visual imagery), the FIN still responds, but its connection with left frontal regions is weaker. Autistic adults report weaker imagery on average, and autism has long been linked to altered long-range brain connectivity, but no study has tested whether autistic people show this aphantasia connectivity pattern. Using resting-state fMRI from ABIDE I (about 1,000 participants across 20 sites), we test whether autistic participants have weaker FIN-to-left-frontoparietal connectivity than non-autistic participants, and whether any difference is larger than the FIN's general difference in connectivity with the rest of the brain. All regions come from a published imagery meta-analysis. ABIDE has no imagery measure, so a positive result would show a shared brain feature, not that it causes weaker imagery. No connectivity value has been computed before registration.

responses.72-2:
Visual mental imagery reliably engages a small region of the left mid-fusiform gyrus, the fusiform imagery node (FIN), together with left frontoparietal regions (Spagna et al., 2021, meta-analysis of 27 fMRI experiments). In congenital aphantasia, the FIN still responds during imagery tasks, but its connectivity with left frontoparietal regions, especially dorsal premotor and prefrontal cortex, is reduced (Liu et al., 2025, Cortex; 7T fMRI, 10 vs 10 participants). Lesions that cause acquired aphantasia are functionally connected to the FIN (Kutsche et al., 2025/2026).

Autistic adults report weaker imagery on average (King et al., 2024; Arnold et al., 2026; Taylor et al., 2026), and autism has long been associated with altered long-range functional connectivity. Kutsche et al. suggested these observations may be linked, but we found no study that tested whether autistic people have reduced FIN-frontoparietal connectivity.

Research question 1: In ABIDE I, do autistic participants have weaker resting-state connectivity between the FIN and left frontoparietal imagery regions than non-autistic participants?
Research question 2: Is any such difference specific to these imagery connections, rather than a general reduction in the FIN's connectivity with the rest of the brain?

Scope: ABIDE has no imagery measure. A positive result would show that autistic brains share a connectivity feature of aphantasia at the group level. It would not show that this feature causes weaker imagery in autistic people.
responses.72-4:
H1 (primary): autistic participants have lower mean FIN-left-frontoparietal connectivity than non-autistic participants. The mean is taken over three prespecified connections (FIN to left parietal, left dorsal premotor and left precentral/middle frontal regions; see Measured variables).

H2 (key secondary, specificity): the autism difference in H1 is larger (more negative) than the autism difference in the FIN's mean connectivity with all other cortical regions.

Other secondary analyses: each of the three connections separately; left versus right hemisphere (the left imagery network compared with its right-hemisphere mirror image); adults only.

H1 predicts a reduction, because the prediction comes from the aphantasia literature. It is nevertheless tested two-sided, because autism connectivity findings run in both directions across studies and ages. An increase would be reported as evidence against the hypothesis.

responses.72-16: ABIDE: Di Martino et al. (2014), Molecular Psychiatry, doi:10.1038/mp.2013.78. ABIDE Preprocessed: Craddock et al. (2013), Frontiers in Neuroinformatics. CC400/CC200 atlases: Craddock et al. (2012), Human Brain Mapping, doi:10.1002/hbm.21333. Spagna et al. (2021), Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, doi:10.1016/j.neubiorev.2020.12.029.
responses.72-20: Data were collected by the ABIDE I sites (20 sites in this release) and shared by ABIDE; we collected no data. Each site acquired resting-state fMRI and structural MRI in autistic and non-autistic participants, with site-specific scanners, protocols and phenotype measures. The Preprocessed Connectomes Project processed all scans with standard pipelines. We use the C-PAC outputs: motion correction, nuisance regression, band-pass filtering, registration to MNI space, and extraction of region-averaged time series for the CC400 and CC200 atlases. Details are in Di Martino et al. (2014) and Craddock et al. (2013).
responses.72-24:
Phenotype variables used: DX_GROUP (1 = autism, 2 = control), AGE_AT_SCAN, SEX (1 = male, 2 = female), SITE_ID, EYE_STATUS_AT_SCAN (1 = open, 2 = closed), func_mean_fd (mean framewise displacement, a measure of head motion, in mm), functional quality ratings (qc_rater_1, qc_func_rater_2, qc_func_rater_3), FIQ (full-scale IQ; values below 0 treated as missing), and for exploratory analyses ADOS_TOTAL, SRS_RAW_TOTAL and AQ_TOTAL (values below 0 treated as missing).

Time-series files: one row per timepoint and one column per atlas region. Column headers are the atlas region numbers (for example, #296); the CC400 files have 392 regions.
responses.72-33:
Group: autism = 1 (DX_GROUP 1), control = 0.

Regions (all from Spagna et al., 2021, visual imagery versus control peaks, MNI x, y, z):
- Seed, the FIN: left mid-fusiform gyrus (-42, -54, -18).
- Left target 1: left inferior parietal lobule / intraparietal sulcus (-40, -44, 46).
- Left target 2: left dorsal premotor / middle frontal gyrus (-26, -2, 60). This is the dorsal premotor region that Liu et al. (2025) found most consistently under-connected to the FIN in aphantasia.
- Left target 3: left precentral / middle frontal gyrus, near the inferior frontal junction (-52, 10, 38).
- Right mirror seed: right mid-fusiform (42, -54, -18).
- Right target 1: right inferior parietal lobule / precuneus (40, -42, 48).
- Right target 2: right middle frontal / precentral gyrus (30, -4, 54).
Other Spagna et al. peaks (supplementary motor area, anterior insula) are not used, because no aphantasia study reports altered FIN connectivity with them.

Each coordinate is assigned to the CC400 region containing it; if it fell outside every region, the nearest region within 6 mm would be used, otherwise the analysis stops. This mapping used only the atlas image and was run before registration: all seven coordinates fall inside separate regions in both CC400 and CC200, and all seven CC400 regions are present in all 1,102 files.

Connection strength: the Pearson correlation between two regions' time series across all timepoints, Fisher-transformed (z = atanh r).
Primary outcome: the mean of the three FIN-left-target z values.
Specificity outcome: the primary outcome minus the FIN's mean z with all other CC400 regions. The average excludes the three targets and any region whose centre is within 20 mm of the FIN, because very close regions share local signal.
Lateralisation outcome: the primary outcome minus the mean of the two right-hemisphere connections.

Covariates: age (linear and squared), sex, mean framewise displacement, eye status at scan (open or closed, which affects visual-cortex connectivity) and site (as fixed effects). Full-scale IQ is not in the primary model (missing at several sites, and possibly on the causal path); an IQ-adjusted model is a sensitivity analysis.
responses.72-35: Participants missing age, sex or eye status are excluded (complete-case). IQ and symptom scores are used only in sensitivity and exploratory analyses, with complete cases. No imputation.
responses.72-39:
Exclusions, applied in this order, with counts reported at each step:
1. No time-series file.
2. Mean framewise displacement above 0.2 mm.
3. Any functional-quality rater marked "fail".
4. Zero or undefined signal variance in any seed or target region.
5. Missing age, sex or eye status.
6. Sites with fewer than 5 participants in either group after steps 1-5 (a site with only one group cannot contribute a within-site comparison).
No other outlier removal. Blind counts already inspected: 884 of the 1,035 participants with files pass step 2 (not broken down by group); 317 of the 1,035 are aged 18 or over.
responses.72-44: ABIDE I data have been used in many published connectivity studies, including studies reporting fusiform connectivity differences in autism. None that we found tested FIN-frontoparietal connectivity or framed the analysis around mental imagery. Before submission we will check any study that used a seed near MNI (-42, -54, -18) in ABIDE and state how our analysis differs.
responses.72-46:
The author knows the published aphantasia and autism literature summarised under Research questions, including that ABIDE autism connectivity findings are mixed and depend on age.

Before registration, only the following were inspected: the phenotype file's column names; counts by diagnosis and site; the overall (not by group) head-motion distribution, quality-rating frequencies and age range; the CC400 and CC200 atlases (for the region mapping); the time-series file headers (to check that all regions are present); and the Spagna et al. coordinate tables.

No connectivity value, and no comparison of any brain measure between autistic and non-autistic participants, has been computed. The analysis code is locked: it will not run until the plan file is frozen (its SHA-256 recorded) and a registration link is supplied. Its tests use synthetic data only.
responses.72-49:
Primary analysis (H1): ordinary least squares (OLS) regression of the primary outcome on the autism indicator, age, age squared, sex, mean framewise displacement, eye status and site (fixed effects), with HC3 robust standard errors. We report the autism coefficient with its 95% CI and a two-sided p-value (alpha = .05). We also report a standardized effect: the coefficient divided by the pooled within-group SD of the outcome.

Secondary analyses (Holm correction across five tests):
1. H2 (specificity): the same model with the specificity outcome.
2-4. The same model for each of the three FIN-left-target connections separately.
5. Lateralisation: the same model with the lateralisation outcome.

Also reported, outside the Holm family:
- Adults only (age 18 or over), because the imagery evidence comes from adults.
- An age-by-autism interaction added to the H1 model, to show whether any difference changes with age.

Software: Python 3.12+ (NumPy, pandas, SciPy); code in src/aphantasia/p7.py of the project repository [ADD PUBLIC REPOSITORY LINK]. Complete plan: preregistration.md, SHA-256 e080e9207783d14d3b86595d0688a331ce9ef90de143c8bdf2ad8d883a4e77e1.
responses.72-51: Autism coefficient in Fisher-z units (difference in connection strength), plus a standardized difference (coefficient divided by the pooled within-group SD). The smallest effect of interest is a standardized difference of 0.15, chosen before analysis and set below the smallest case-control connectivity differences typically reported in ABIDE.
responses.72-53: With about 400 participants per group after exclusions (a rough expectation; exact counts are fixed by the exclusion rules) and two-sided alpha = .05, power is about 0.80 for a standardized difference of 0.20 and about 0.55 for 0.15. Site effects and covariates will change this slightly. The adults-only analysis has much lower power (roughly 250 participants) and is treated as descriptive.
responses.72-55:
Interpretation, fixed in advance:
1. H1 below zero with a CI excluding 0, and H2 below zero with a CI excluding 0: autistic participants show reduced FIN-frontoparietal connectivity beyond the FIN's general connectivity difference. This is consistent with sharing aphantasia's connectivity feature.
2. H1 below zero with a CI excluding 0, but H2's CI including 0: reduced connectivity, but not specific to the imagery network; consistent with general long-range differences in connectivity.
3. H1's CI including 0: no evidence of the aphantasia connectivity signature. We also run an equivalence test (two one-sided tests, bounds of plus or minus 0.15 SD) and report whether effects of that size can be ruled out.
4. H1 above zero with a CI excluding 0: increased connectivity, reported as evidence against this pathway.
responses.72-57: If a prespecified coordinate is more than 6 mm from every atlas region, or two coordinates fall in the same region, the analysis stops and a deviation is recorded. A participant whose seed or target region has no signal is excluded (step 4). Robust (HC3) standard errors are used, so non-constant variance does not require a model change. If a model cannot be estimated, it is reported as not estimable, with the reason. Any departure from this plan is logged in a dated deviations file stating whether results had been seen, and reported in the paper.
responses.72-59:
Sensitivity analyses for the primary outcome (all reported):
1. Global signal regression pipeline (cpac/filt_global/rois_cc400).
2. Stricter head-motion threshold (mean framewise displacement 0.1 mm or less), and no motion exclusion.
3. CC200 atlas instead of CC400.
4. Adjustment for full-scale IQ (complete cases).
5. Males only (ABIDE I is predominantly male).
6. Leave-one-site-out: the range of the autism coefficient across refits.
7. Site handled by site-clustered standard errors instead of site fixed effects.
responses.72-61: Within autistic participants: associations of the primary outcome with ADOS total and SRS total scores, where available (at least 30 participants required). Association of the primary outcome with AQ total at the sites that collected it. A full FIN connectivity profile across all CC400 regions, with maps of autism-minus-control differences. These are exploratory and carry no inferential claims.
responses.72-29: None. This is an observational secondary analysis of existing data.
